transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Luis (Redwood CSM), Marcus (Elysian Head of Platform), Anita (Elysian ML Eng), Sanjay (CTO), Leah (SRE)

Summary: quick review of week-2 bench numbers vs their incumbent baseline, discussed routing/quantization tradeoffs, agreed to a 24h dedicated soak on H100, and decided next steps for security paperwork and baseline load share.

Topics: latency/throughput comparison, tail (p99/p999) behavior, batch sizing, KV/prefix caching, model-variant routing for graceful fallback, dedicated slot soak test, security docs and network peering.

Action items (captured verbally in call): see metadata action_items list above.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. quick context — this is our week-2 sync to go over the benchmark numbers we ran against your baseline provider and call out tuning we did overnight. priya will walk through the raw numbers.
[00:18] Priya: yeah hi um so we ran the two main scenarios you gave us: 1) low-latency single-request profile (1-2 tokens after prompt) and 2) long-seq throughput (avg 1,200 tokens per request) to reflect your document summarize flow. i have slides in the doc but i'll read the highlights.
[00:36] Marcus: sounds good, please focus on the tail stats — that's what our product cares about, p95/p99.
[00:44] Priya: right. for the single-request profile on H100 with Redwood runtime + quant 4-bit opt, median latency was ~95ms, p95 was ~180ms, p99 240ms. your incumbent baseline reported median 180ms, p95 330ms, p99 520ms in their report — we reproduced those numbers using your k6 script.
[01:10] Anita: quick clarification, are those numbers with KV cache warmed? in some of our earlier runs the cache cold starts were awful.
[01:18] Priya: good question — these single-request numbers were with prefix caching enabled and a warmed KV in most runs. cold-starts for previously unseen prefixes did add ~150-300ms on first token but that's expected, and we have cache hit logs attached.
[01:34] Sanjay: how noisy is the p99 — like network egress or infra noise?
[01:38] Priya: some of it is infra jitter we saw on a tiny percentage of requests, we correlated with peak network egress in the host. we also noticed the baseline's p99 had a larger spread — looks like their multi-tenant placement and CPU contention influence.
[01:55] Jordan: to add, the dedicated slot soak we propose is to remove placement noise and prove steady-state tail numbers. that's why we want a 24-hour run on a dedicated H100.
[02:06] Leah: ok that'd be useful. for the long-sequence throughput test what did you see?
[02:12] Priya: for the 1,200 token average flows on 8 concurrent streams per GPU: Redwood sustained ~2.1k tokens/sec per GPU with median token latency of ~8ms (per token), effective end-to-end per-request completion time was about 580ms. the baseline in your benchmark averaged ~1.3k tokens/sec and per-request completion times ~950-1,100ms. throughput scaling with batching was more efficient for our runtime.
[02:39] Marcus: that's promising. can you remind us of the beam/quant settings here? i remember seeing mixed quant levels in the config.
[02:46] Priya: sure — we used int4 quant for the model weights and per-layer kernel selection optimized for long sequences; dynamic batching up to 64 tokens per batch, continuous batching enabled in the runtime. we also toggled a routing policy to send latency-sensitive small requests to a lower-batch, low-latency execution path.
[03:05] Anita: the routing policy is interesting — can you explain how the split works? we don't want messages shuffled to a slower path during spikes.
[03:12] Priya: absolutely. policy is request-aware: based on request size, user-specified latency SLO, and current queueing, router will pick either the low-batch low-latency pod or the high-batch high-throughput pod. we also configured an automatic fallback — if the low-latency pool is saturated beyond threshold it spills over to the throughput pool but with a hard limit and circuit-breaker to avoid large latency cliffs.
[03:35] Sanjay: do you have per-route SLOs? we need per-API key SLA to be enforced.
[03:40] Jordan: yes, Redwood Console supports per-route SLOs and token-level cost accounting — we'll share a sample route config that maps your production keys to the low-latency pool.
[03:48] Marcus: cost question — how does the quant + batching impact cost vs baseline? our CFO will ask.
[03:54] Jordan: short answer: quant + efficient batching reduces token compute by ~30-40% in our profiles, that roughly translates to 25-35% lower per-token cost vs the baseline in these workloads. we'll put a cost comparison spreadsheet in the shared folder.
[04:08] Anita: small nit — earlier we saw an artifact where K-V cache hits were counted as cache misses in your dashboard; is that a dashboard bug or something wrong in the runtime?
[04:16] Priya: we dug into this — some logs had a mismatch because our log parser expects a header that your baseline load generator didn't include; it's a parsing mismatch, not a runtime miss. we've patched the parser and rebuilt the dashboard ingest for the spreadsheet attached.
[04:31] Leah: for VPC/on-prem tests, network egress and MTU sizing were concerns. can you replicate realistic peering?
[04:38] Priya: yes, we can run the dedicated slot in your VPC via our Private deployment if you want full parity; for this soak run we propose using Redwood's dedicated in-region H100 to isolate placement noise, and then follow with a VPC-peered soak when network configs are validated.
[04:56] Jordan: quick product note — during the soak we'll also enable observability hooks so you get fine-grained token-level traces and a sample of failed completions for QA.
[05:06] Marcus: perfect. about the long-tail p999 — your slides showed ~520ms while baseline had 1.1s — can you explain the main contributors?
[05:14] Priya: p999 is driven by two sources: 1) cold-cache prefix misses and 2) scheduling outliers due to multi-tenant interference. our dedicated runtime reduces #2; caching and pre-warming heuristics help with #1. we recommended pre-warming frequent prefixes during business hours to avoid first-hit latencies.
[05:33] Anita: can Redwood run pre-warm as a background job? we have millions of possible prefixes, but a focused set of ~5k top prefixes is realistic.
[05:40] Priya: yes, we can add a pre-warm job that touches those prefixes in KV cache ahead of traffic windows. it can run as a scheduled job via the Console.
[05:48] Sanjay: security checklist — we still need SOC2 link, SAML SSO flow, and encryption at rest details. Jordan?
[05:55] Jordan: i'll drop our SOC2 PDF and an SSO integration guide in the shared folder today, and priya will annotate any config changes needed for SAML.
[06:03] Marcus: excellent. about the baseline reproducibility — we noticed the baseline vendor throttled at 1.8k tokens/sec in one run, not consistent across runs. did you have rate limiting applied?
[06:12] Priya: for parity we mirrored your k6 script which has a ramp pattern and a hard concurrency cap. we also injected occasional background noise to simulate multi-tenant traffic. the throttling you saw is consistent with the baseline's reported autoscaler behavior. Redwood's dedicated slot maintains steady throughput because we control isolation and autoscale policies.
[06:33] Leah: can we get the raw logs for the soak? we want to run our in-house tail-analysis script.
[06:37] Jordan: yes we'll provide logs — note that the logs include UUIDs we can mask for PII before handing off.
[06:44] Anita: one more technical: quantization introduced slight quality drift on a subset of prompts; the evals you ran earlier flagged 1.8% regression on extraction tasks. is there a tuning knob?
[06:55] Priya: we saw the regression too. mitigation options: 1) per-layer mixed-precision for critical layers (reduces speedup a bit), 2) apply 8-bit to specific layers, or 3) serve a higher-fidelity model variant for extraction routes and route other traffic to quantized variant. routing-by-intent is fully supported.
[07:17] Sanjay: routing-by-intent sounds interesting — we'd like to route extraction API to high-fidelity variant. what is the cost delta?
[07:23] Jordan: roughly 40-60% more compute for high-fidelity per-token than int4 quant; but because extraction is only ~12% of your calls, the overall bill impact is modest. we'll model that in the cost spreadsheet.
[07:37] Marcus: good. let's lock the soak parameters — what do you need from us?
[07:41] Priya: we need your baseline k6 script, sequence length histogram, and a production-ish API key for canary routing. also confirm peak concurrency you want simulated.
[07:51] Anita: we'll send the k6 script and histogram by Friday (2026-08-14). peak concurrency is 120 RPS with the long-seq distribution.
[07:58] Jordan: noted. we'll schedule the dedicated soak starting 2026-08-15 and run for 24 hours, then hand the logs to you and circulate the soak dashboard.
[08:06] Leah: network-wise, we'll validate the VPC peering IAM roles by 2026-08-16.
[08:11] Jordan: great. any other blockers?
[08:14] Marcus: only question — competitive differentiation. your slides compared end-to-end latency but not developer ergonomics; can we get a small demo of the rollout and fallback console?
[08:23] Jordan: yes we can schedule a 30-min run-through next week; luis will set that up.
[08:29] Luis: i'll send a calendar invite for a 30-min Redwood Console demo and a follow-up on security paperwork.
[08:36] Anita: thanks — small note, please include logs for the quant A/B split so we can see per-prompt fuzz.
[08:41] Priya: will do. we'll also attach per-route QA samples for the 1.8% regression so your team can triage.
[08:47] Sanjay: ok that covers it, appreciate the throughput uplift. look forward to the soak.
[08:52] Jordan: thanks everyone — recap in the doc and action items in the spreadsheet. we'll follow up on the shared folder.
[08:57] Marcus: thanks all. bye.

End of call.
